query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high-entropy alloy, specifically a tungsten-based alloy (e.g., a NbMoTaW alloy), can be applied as a coating to a Cu matrix and will adhere well due to favorable interfacial bonding mechanisms and similar thermal compatibility, leading to markedly improved surface wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A Cu matrix with its native surface properties (uncoated, with typical wear and friction characteristics).
generation.intervention: Deposit a refractory high-entropy alloy coating (NbMoTaW, which is tungsten-based) onto the surface of the Cu matrix using an appropriate coating or deposition technique.
generation.conditions: Room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures under mechanical wear conditions, where the Cu substrate normally exhibits limited wear resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent interfacial layer between the Cu substrate and the BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloy that aids in mechanical interlocking and intermetallic bonding.
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy alloy’s intrinsic high wear resistance and its potential for forming a chemically compatible, thermally matched interface with copper facilitate robust adhesion. This interfacial layer minimizes delamination under cyclic loading and abrasion, thereby enhancing surface protection.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated Cu matrix will display significantly improved wear resistance and sustained coating integrity compared to the uncoated Cu substrate, with reduced wear rates and improved performance under cyclic mechanical stresses.
generation.baseline: The wear performance and adhesion characteristics of an uncoated Cu matrix under identical environmental and mechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to situations where the deposition process can produce a uniform and defect-minimized high-entropy alloy coating, and under conditions where thermal expansion mismatch does not induce excessive stress at the interface.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of adhesion improvement and wear resistance enhancement depends on the detailed interfacial chemistry and microstructure, which may vary with deposition parameters and environmental conditions. The long-term stability of the interface under extreme wear or thermal cycling also remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Cu samples, half coated with the tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW) via a controlled deposition technique, and half left uncoated. Subject both sample sets to a standardized series of wear tests, including scratch tests to evaluate coating adhesion and wear rate measurements under controlled cyclic mechanical loading. Monitor the interfacial microstructure using microscopy techniques before and after testing.
measurements: Scratch adhesion strength (quantified force at delamination)
Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss per cycle)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated Cu samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in wear resistance and adhesion strength compared to the uncoated controls—or if the interface shows rapid degradation under the test conditions—the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
